entities.name: Teudebur of Alt Clut
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Teudebur of Alt Clut, who reigned until his death in 752 CE, was a pivotal monarch of the Brittonic kingdom of Alt Clut (Strathclyde) during a period of intense geopolitical flux in early medieval Britain. Identified in the Harleian genealogies as the son of Beli II, Teudebur's rule saw Alt Clut navigate the formidable expansionist ambitions of the neighboring Pictish kingdom under Óengus mac Fergusa, a critical struggle for sovereignty that profoundly shaped the political landscape of northern Britain. His reign represents a key phase in the kingdom's resistance against external pressures, maintaining a distinct Brittonic identity amidst consolidating Anglo-Saxon and Pictish powers.

The precise chronology of Teudebur's ascension is unknown, but his reign is securely placed in the early-to-mid eighth century, culminating in his death in 752 CE, as attested by the Irish and Welsh annals. A defining moment of his kingship was the Battle of Mocetauc in 750 CE, where the Annales Cambriae records a significant victory for the Britons against the Picts. This engagement, likely a direct confrontation with Óengus mac Fergusa's forces, temporarily checked Pictish expansion westwards and secured Alt Clut's borders, at least for a time. Teudebur's success in this conflict demonstrates a strategic military capability that allowed Alt Clut to maintain its independence against one of the most powerful rulers of the era.
